paragraphs.source_en: There are two possible ways in which stones from this area could have reached the territory of the Round Heads. Firstly, the groups may have travelled directly into the territory occupied by groups of another culture, with whom they had good relationships judging by the raw material obtained from them. The mobility of groups between neighbouring territories is documented ethnographically amongst numerous huntergatherers, for example the ! Kung San who move to the other groups' territory in order to visit relatives, to socialize or to exchange goods (Lee & De Vore 1976). Secondly, it is possible that there was an exchange of goods between neighbouring groups in a "free-zone". Groups of different cultures would have not entered their neighbours' territory but they would have met in a neutral place in order to exchange items or perhaps to socialize.

paragraphs.source_en: Interestingly, the situation changed in the later Mesolithic phase. Even though the occupation of sites was continuous and the economy was still based on wild animals and wild plants, the frequency of the "exotic" raw materials falls sharply. High quality materials diminished, with a low incidence of quartzite, whilst quartz and flint almost disappeared (Di Lernia 1999). This period, starting from around 8,500 BP, experienced drier climatic conditions but it does not seem to be the main reason for people to stop searching for materials which were previously very popular. Possible reasons for this may be that either the groups stopped travelling large distances, or that the contacts (and therefore exchanges) between the neighbouring groups ceased.

paragraphs.source_en: - it appears almost simultaneously in various (and distant) regions, - it presents a similar decoration in all regions, - the same decoration remains immutable for more than 2,000 years.
